extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedians, comedy students, and general readers interested in stand-up comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for writing, delivering, and staging live stand-up comedy routines, including show roles, joke structures, delivery techniques, audience interaction, and ethical/social norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine construction (premise, set-up, punchline, closer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines are constructed and refined with jokes and interconnected 'bits.' Many jokes are the juxtaposition of two incongruous things and are made up of the premise, set-up, and punchline, often adding a twist, topper, or tagline for an intensified or extra laugh. Bits form an interwoven narrative, leading to the 'closer,' the final joke that ties the show's themes together for a satisfying conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop interconnected bits that build toward a satisfying closer; use twists, toppers, and taglines to intensify laughs. Treat the routine as an interwoven narrative rather than isolated jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery: intonation, inflection, attitude, timing (beat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery relies on the use of intonation, inflection, attitude, and timing as well as other stylistic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pauses ('beat') to create comic timing. Tone and pace are as important as written material; refine delivery to maximize the payoff of the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure devices (rule of three, paraprosdokian, wordplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic devices such as the rule of three, idioms, archetypes, wordplay, and the paraprosdokian (a surprising punchline that changes the meaning of the setup) are common joke-structure tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ these devices deliberately to shape expectations and subvert them for comedic effect; the paraprosdokian is noted as a popular structure for surprising punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre/style selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up has multiple genres and styles with their formats (examples listed: Alternative/alt-comedy, Anecdotal, Character, Deadpan, Impressionist, Insult, Musical, Observational, Satire, Topical, Wordplay, Self-Deprecating, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a style that fits your voice and material; genres carry different expectations (e.g., alt-comedy often counters the set-up/punchline approach; insult comedy targets the audience/other performers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interaction and 'crowdwork'
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances often include live crowd interaction (crowdwork). Audiences are 'co-constructors' and 'co-responsible' for the situation; an unspoken contract allows exploration of unexpected or controversial subjects. A seasoned comic reacts instantly to audience reaction and uses it to further the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and 'work the room'; adapt material on the fly based on audience response. Success is measured by audience laughter—'If the audience is not laughing, the joke is not working.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Show roles and set-slot structure (emcee, opener, feature, headliner)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a typical stand-up show, the host/emcee warms up the audience and introduces other performers. This is followed by the opener, the feature, and then the headliner. On the circuit, headliner does roughly an hour of original material, the feature does 25–30 minutes, the opener has a ten minute slot, and the emcee squeezes in a joke or two between acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure your material to fit the expected slot length and role; emcees focus on warm-up, openers deliver short tight sets, features do longer curated sets, and headliners carry the show with an hour of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open mic and 'work out' process
rubrics_metrics.description: Open mics are used by comedians to work on material or to show off skills to get an opener slot. 'Work out' is the process in which brand new jokes are introduced and polished over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open mics and frequent performing to test, refine, and polish new material; be aware of bringer shows where performers bring paying guests to get stage time.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV special and album runtimes
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'half-hour special' is typically between 20 and 35 minutes in runtime excluding commercial breaks and an 'hour-long special' is typically between 40 and 65 minutes excluding commercial breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan recorded specials to fit these typical runtimes when preparing material for television, streaming, or album release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical elements and prop use (act outs, props, impressions, music, magic, ventriloquism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up can incorporate physical acts (act outs), props, music, impressions, dialects, magic tricks, or ventriloquism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate physical elements judiciously to support rather than distract from verbal material; different venues/audiences respond differently to props and physical comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/social guidance: punching up vs punching down
rubrics_metrics.description: The concepts of 'punching up' and 'punching down' describe who should be the 'butt of the joke'—the assumption is that comedy should 'punch up' at the rich and powerful without 'punching down' at marginalized or less fortunate groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider power dynamics and potential harm when selecting targets for jokes; note that this is culturally debated and not universally accepted among comedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke theft and appropriation (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation and plagiarism are considered 'social crimes' by most stand-ups. There have been high-profile accusations of joke theft; accused comedians may claim cryptomnesia or parallel thinking, but it is difficult to successfully sue due to the idea–expression distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using others' material; maintain originality and acknowledge influences. Understand legal/ethical limits but prioritize professional norms against theft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance aims: spontaneity, intimacy, and heckle management
rubrics_metrics.description: Success hinges on creating spontaneity, fostering intimacy, and deterring heckling. The audience is integral as foil and contributor to the experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an atmosphere of immediacy and rapport; prepare strategies to deter and handle hecklers while maintaining the show's flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tight five and reliable short-form material
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tight five' is a five-minute routine that is well-rehearsed and consists of a comedian's best material that reliably gets laughs; it is often used for auditions and is a stepping stone to getting a paid spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a tight, dependable short set for auditions and club opportunities; ensure material in the tight five is highly polished and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology as diagnostic vocabulary (bombing, callback, clapter, corpsing, mugging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as 'bombing' (failing to get laughs), 'callback' (reference to earlier joke), 'clapter' (applause for an opinion rather than a joke), 'corpsing' (comedian laughing unintentionally), and 'mugging' (pulling silly faces) describe performance phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concepts to diagnose performance problems and successes; e.g., reduce mugging, learn from bombs, and deploy callbacks intentionally to build laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of canned laughter and filming considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Canned laughter in television comedy reveals the audience's role; shows may be filmed in front of a live audience for the same reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing material for recorded formats, account for differences between live audience dynamics and recorded/edited presentation; consider how canned laughter or lack thereof affects pacing and perceived funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of festivals and touring for career development
rubrics_metrics.description: Festivals showcase up-and-coming acts and are used by promoters and agents to seek out new talent. Proven comics earn regular bookings at club chains and venues; jobbing stand-ups may perform multiple sets/venues per day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use festivals to gain exposure and industry attention; build relationships with venues and promoters to secure regular bookings.
